title: How many get through the turnstile?
hook: A locked turnstile, six events, a few people. Count who gets through.

doesNotKnow: that a machine can remember only which state it is in, not a count

misconception: The turnstile counts coins, so two coins in a row buy two passes.
objective: The learner can trace a two-state machine: on coin, push, push, coin, coin, push from locked, 2 people pass, because the second coin in a row changes nothing.

claims.text: A turnstile that starts locked and receives coin, push, push, coin, coin, push lets 2 people through.
claims.source: Demo.tsx run(6): passed = 2. Builder re-ran the trace in Node with an independent loop: 2. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Node: coin, push, push, coin, coin, push from Locked passes 2 people.

claims.text: In this turnstile a coin unlocks it, a push while unlocked lets one person through and locks it, a push while locked is blocked, and a coin while unlocked changes nothing.
claims.source: The rules of the standard coin-operated turnstile example (Wikipedia, 'Finite-state machine', section 'Example: coin-operated turnstile', state-transition table). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Matches the standard coin-operated turnstile table.

claims.text: On this run the second coin in a row (event 5) found the turnstile already unlocked and changed nothing.
claims.source: Demo.tsx run(5).edge = 'coin-wasted'; WASTED_AT = 5. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Re-derived; no issue.

claims.text: The turnstile counts nothing: its whole memory is which of its two states it is in.
claims.source: Follows from c2: the next state depends only on the current state and the event; the model stores no other value. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Re-derived; no issue.

claims.text: A finite-state machine has fixed states and a rule for each event in each state.
claims.source: Sipser, Introduction to the Theory of Computation, 3rd ed., Definition 1.5 (finite automaton: finite set of states, alphabet, transition function, start state, accept states). Lesson wording is the informal reading; accept states are omitted. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Sipser 3rd ed. Definition 1.5 is the finite automaton definition; the lesson omits accept states and says so.

recall.question: A door lock has two states. Entering the code unlocks it; opening the door lets you in and locks it again. Events from locked: code, code, open, open. How many entries?
recall.why: The second code finds it already unlocked and is lost; the first open lets one person in and locks it, so the second open is blocked.
